paragraphs.heading: What a fern is
paragraphs.text: Ferns are vascular plants that spread by spores and have no seeds and no flowers. More than 10,500 species are alive today. As in seed plants, the fern's sporophyte, the stage of its life that makes spores, is made of stems, leaves and roots. Ferns differ from lycophytes, another group of spore-bearing plants, in having true leaves.

paragraphs.heading: Fronds and fiddleheads
paragraphs.text: The green part of a fern that does photosynthesis is technically a megaphyll, a leaf more complex than a clubmoss microphyll. In ferns it is often called a frond. In leptosporangiate ferns, a new leaf generally starts as a tight spiral called a crozier or fiddlehead and unrolls into a frond. Botanists call this uncurling circinate vernation. Living ferns are herbaceous perennials, and most have no woody growth; where wood does occur, it is in the stem. Depending on the climate, their foliage may be deciduous, evergreen or semi-evergreen.

paragraphs.heading: A life in two stages
paragraphs.text: A fern's life cycle has two stages, as in clubmosses and horsetails. First, a spore sprouts into a short-lived gametophyte called the prothallus, which makes sperm and eggs. It is held to the soil by rhizoids, root-like structures made of single, very long cells that soak up water and mineral salts. Second, a sporophyte grows, depends on the gametophyte only briefly, then lives on its own and carries spores on fertile fronds. The sporophyte is the dominant stage, just as it is in every vascular plant.

paragraphs.heading: Sperm that swims
paragraphs.text: The gametophyte develops from the spore by mitosis, a kind of cell division that keeps the number of chromosomes the same. Using mitosis, the prothallus then forms small round antheridia that hold sperm and flask-shaped archegonia that each release a single egg. The flagellate sperm swims down the neck of an archegonium and fertilizes the egg. The egg stays attached to the prothallus and grows by mitosis into a diploid zygote, which becomes the sporophyte. The prothallus lasts only a short while after that.

paragraphs.heading: Full sets and half sets
paragraphs.text: The sporophyte is diploid: it has 2n paired chromosomes, where n depends on the species. The gametophyte is haploid, with n unpaired chromosomes, half as many. The sporophyte makes haploid spores by meiosis, a cell division that halves the chromosome number. A mature frond releases them from sori, clusters of sporangia (the cases that hold spores) on its underside. The sporangia may wear a protective cover called an indusium, and how they are arranged matters for classifying ferns.

paragraphs.heading: Old group, young branches, weeds
paragraphs.text: The fern group as a whole is thought to date from about 423 million years ago, in the late Silurian. Yet the Polypodiales, which make up 80% of the ferns living now, only appeared and spread in the Cretaceous, about 143 to 66 million years ago, while flowering plants were also diversifying fast. Some ferns, such as bracken and water fern, are serious weeds around the world, and brackens can cause cancer. Ferns matter little to the economy, but some are eaten, used as medicine or grown as ornamentals.
